reference.source: Williams Obstetrics / Novak's Gynecology / Campbell-Walsh Urology
clinicalPearls: Placenta accreta spectrum describes abnormal trophoblastic invasion into or through the uterine wall, graded as accreta (adherent to myometrium), increta (invading myometrium), and percreta (penetrating serosa and sometimes adjacent organs such as the bladder)
The dominant risk factors are a previous caesarean scar combined with a placenta praevia overlying that scar; risk rises steeply with each additional caesarean delivery

Antenatal diagnosis is largely by ultrasound, with features such as loss of the retroplacental clear zone, placental lacunae, and disruption of the bladder-uterine interface; MRI is a useful adjunct when posterior placentation or bladder involvement is suspected
Attempted separation of an adherent placenta at delivery provokes torrential, life-threatening haemorrhage, so the management principle is to avoid forced removal
Planned delivery in a specialist multidisciplinary centre, typically by scheduled preterm caesarean with the placenta left in situ and caesarean hysterectomy, gives the best maternal outcomes
Preparation includes large-bore venous access, cross-matched blood and a massive transfusion protocol, cell salvage where available, and involvement of urology and interventional radiology
Percreta invading the bladder may require urological support for cystotomy repair or ureteric stenting, hence multidisciplinary planning is essential
Conservative uterus-preserving approaches exist but carry risks of delayed haemorrhage, infection, and the need for later intervention, so they are reserved for selected cases
Any woman with placenta praevia and a prior uterine scar should be actively screened for accreta rather than assumed to have simple praevia
reference.pathophysiology: The disorder arises from a defect in the decidua basalis, usually within a uterine scar, so that the normal Nitabuch fibrinoid layer that limits trophoblast invasion is deficient or absent. Chorionic villi therefore anchor directly onto or into the myometrium instead of the decidua. The depth of invasion determines the grade. Scar tissue is poorly vascularised and lacks a decidual cleavage plane, so at delivery the placenta cannot separate physiologically; disruption of the abnormal placental-myometrial interface tears richly vascular tissue and causes massive obstetric haemorrhage. Neovascularisation around the invasion front contributes to the bleeding risk.
additionalDifferentials: Simple placenta praevia without abnormal invasion
additionalInvestigations: Detailed obstetric ultrasound including transvaginal assessment of the lower segment and colour Doppler of the placental bed
Pelvic MRI when depth of invasion, posterior placentation, or bladder/parametrial involvement is uncertain
Full blood count and baseline coagulation screen
Blood group, antibody screen, and cross-match with activation of a massive transfusion pathway
Cystoscopy or urological assessment where bladder invasion (percreta) is suspected
Anaesthetic and critical care review as part of multidisciplinary planning
redFlags: OBSTETRIC EMERGENCY: catastrophic intrapartum or postpartum haemorrhage on attempted placental separation requiring immediate massive transfusion and surgical control
Haemodynamic instability, tachycardia, and hypotension indicating major blood loss
Placenta percreta with bladder or bowel involvement risking visceral injury and uncontrolled bleeding
Coagulopathy or disseminated intravascular coagulation complicating massive transfusion
Unplanned delivery outside a specialist centre without blood products or surgical backup
reference.prognosis: With antenatal diagnosis and planned management in an experienced multidisciplinary unit, maternal survival is high and morbidity is reduced, though many women require hysterectomy and lose future fertility. Undiagnosed cases presenting acutely carry a substantially higher risk of massive haemorrhage, intensive care admission, visceral injury, and maternal death. Recurrence risk relates to the underlying scarring and future uterine surgery.
pitfalls: Failing to screen for accreta in a woman with placenta praevia and a previous caesarean scar
Attempting to deliver the placenta manually and precipitating uncontrolled haemorrhage
Delivering in a non-specialist setting without blood products, cell salvage, or surgical support
Underestimating bladder involvement in percreta and omitting urological planning
Assuming a conservative uterus-preserving approach is low risk when delayed haemorrhage and sepsis can follow
management: Planned preterm caesarean delivery in a specialist multidisciplinary centre with the placenta left in situ
Caesarean hysterectomy as the definitive procedure, avoiding forced placental separation
Preparation for major haemorrhage with large-bore venous access, cross-matched blood, a massive transfusion protocol and cell salvage
Antenatal corticosteroids for foetal lung maturity before scheduled preterm delivery
Interventional radiology for prophylactic balloon occlusion or embolisation and urology involvement, with ureteric stents where bladder invasion is suspected
Uterus-preserving expectant management with the placenta left in place only in carefully selected women wishing to retain fertility
Postoperative critical care, thromboprophylaxis and monitoring for delayed haemorrhage and infection
Counselling on likely loss of fertility with multidisciplinary planning
